title: A Plan on a Napkin

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 12: A plan is just a decision written down so you can argue with it.*

The mess hall was empty, save for the hum of the ventilation fans and the clatter of a single spoon against a ceramic bowl. The table was a battlefield of grease-stained napkins, half-eaten cheese sandwiches, and a large, dented pot of lentil soup that smelled of cumin and iron. Chief Engineer Bram Voss sat at the head, his bushy ginger beard shadowing the lower half of his face, while Kess, Lio, and Pim crowded onto the benches opposite. Mr. Daro, a retired welder with hands like knotted rope, sat to Voss’s right, nursing a cup of tea that had gone cold.

Voss had taken a napkin from the dispenser, unfolded it, and with a grease-stained marker, sketched a sprawling web of lines. It was not a map of the ship, but a map of the radiator loop, a tangled artery of coolant pipes that ran from the reactor core to the vast silver wings outside. He tapped a specific junction with his thick finger, a point where three lines converged into one.

"This is the manifold," Voss said, his voice low and rough. "The cold panel is on this branch. We cannot fix it while it is flowing. We need to stop the flow." He drew two small circles on the lines, one before the junction and one after. "Isolation valves. We close these, cut out the failed section, and install a bypass. Simple, in theory."

Pim leaned forward, his yellow hair ties bouncing. "But the valve is stuck. We tried. It seized up years ago."

"Then we do not use the valve," Voss said, not looking up. "We use the pump. We throttle the main pump down to a trickle, isolate the branch with the manual override on the pump house floor, and we pray that the pressure drop is enough to keep the heat from building up in the isolated section while we work. It is tight. But it is possible."

Kess watched the lines on the napkin. They looked like the root system of an apple tree, except that instead of drawing water and nutrients, they were drawing heat, and if they broke, the ship would boil. She picked up the marker, hesitated, and then added a small circle at the end of the bypass line. "And here," she said. "A check valve. So the coolant doesn't flow backward into the reactor if the pump stalls."

Voss looked at her, then at the circle. He did not smile, but the tension in his shoulders dropped, just a fraction. "Good eye, kid. You think like a plumber."

"I think like a gardener," Kess corrected. "You just need to know where the water wants to go."

Lio, who had been quiet, spoke up. "The problem is, we can't reach the joint from inside. The panel is on the exterior. To cut it out, we have to go out there."

The room went quiet. The hum of the fans seemed to grow louder, filling the spaces between their words.
pages.image: A crowded mess hall table at night with five people: a bearded engineer, a girl with a silver hair streak, a tall boy in a navy jumpsuit, a small boy in a red hoodie, and an older man, all leaning over a grease-stained napkin with a hand-drawn diagram of pipes.

pages.text:
"Going out there is not a suggestion," Lio said, his voice steady though his hands were clasped tightly between his knees. "It is a requirement. The joint is on the exterior face of the wing, and there is no internal access point. We need an EVA suit, a pipe cutter, and a clamp-on patch sleeve."

Mr. Daro leaned forward, his tea cup trembling slightly in his hand as his eyes brightened with a focused, sudden energy. "I have a sleeve design," he said. "From my welding days. It uses a flexible composite material that expands under pressure. You don't need to weld it in place. You just clamp it over the joint, and it seals itself. It is safer than welding in a vacuum, and it does not require the same level of precision."

Kess looked at him, then at the grease-stained napkin on the table. "That sounds... optimistic."

"It is practical," Daro corrected, a faint smile touching his lips. "I have used it on small ships. It holds. But you have to test it. You cannot just put it on the ship and hope for the best. You need to know that it can handle the pressure differential."

Pim raised his hand, as if in a classroom, though the only teacher present was a bowl of cold lentil soup. "We can test it in the Orchard's cooling pond loop," he said. "It is a closed system. We can simulate the pressure drop. If it holds there, it will hold out there."

Kess blinked. "The cooling pond is for the trees. It is not a pressure test chamber."

"It is a closed loop of water under pressure," Pim insisted, his yellow hair ties bouncing with each emphatic word. "The physics is the same. If the sleeve can hold back the water in the pond, it can hold back the coolant in the wing. And if it fails, we just drain the pond. We do not lose the ship."

Voss looked at Pim, then at the napkin, and finally at Kess. "The boy is right. It is a low-risk test. We can set it up in the workshop. We use a section of pipe from the scrap heap. We run water through it. We apply the sleeve. We pressurize it."

"It is a good idea," Kess said, and she meant it. It was the first time in days that she had heard a solution that did not end with "we need more time" or "we need more parts." It was a solution that was already there, waiting to be used, like a graft that had finally taken hold.

Lio nodded slowly, his gaze drifting to the lamp on the wall, which was glowing a steady, warm amber. "I can build the test rig. I have the parts. I just need the authorization to use the workshop for the night."

Voss looked at the lamp, then back to the group. "Authorization is not the problem," he said. "The problem is the time. We have twenty-three days until the vote. We need to get this done, tested, and installed before then."
pages.image: An older man with a white beard gestures toward a small, flexible metal sleeve while a girl with a silver hair streak and a small boy in a red hoodie listen intently, a workshop bench with tools visible in the background.

pages.text:
Kess took the marker and drew a firm line under the bypass section of the schematic. "Here is the catch," she said, tapping the spot where the coolant loop would be sealed. "When we isolate that branch, the wing loses a percent of its cooling capacity. For the duration of the repair, the ship's power margin drops to two point one percent. If we do not compensate, the reactor will throttle down. And if the reactor throttles down, the Orchard's grow-lights will brown out."

The table went quiet again, but this time it was a different kind of quiet, the sort that settles over a workshop when a heavy press finally locks into place. It was the silence of a decision being made, of gears meshing after a long period of grinding against each other.

"Dimming the lights," Lio said, his voice flat and careful.

"Temporarily," Kess replied. "Just for the repair. Maybe a few hours. The trees can handle a brief drop in light. They have survived worse. But it is a trade-off. We are not killing the Orchard to save the ship. We are using the Orchard's sacrifice to buy time to save the ship. And if the repair works, we turn the lights back on. And if the repair fails, we have lost nothing we did not already have to lose."

Voss looked at her, and for the first time, he seemed to see her not as a kid, but as a partner. "You are turning a loss into a lever," he said, his ginger beard twitching as he chewed on the logic.

"I am turning a tragedy into a transaction," Kess said, leaning back against her chair. "Tally can accept a transaction. It cannot accept a tragedy. It is all about the arithmetic."

Pim frowned, his yellow hair ties bouncing slightly as he shook his head. "But the trees will be sad."

"The trees will be fine," Kess said gently. "They are tougher than us. They have been growing under lamps for two hundred years. They will understand."

Lio looked at Kess, and there was something in his eyes that she had not seen before. It was not fear, exactly. It was recognition. He was seeing her not as the girl who climbed trees, but as the person who understood the system. And she was seeing him not as the boy who hummed while he worked, but as the person who could make the system work.

"We need to tell Tally," Kess said, standing up and brushing a crumb from her coverall. "We need to tell it that we have a plan. And we need to tell it that the Orchard is not being cut. It is being spared. There is a difference."

Voss nodded, reaching for his tea cup with a steadier hand than before. "I will talk to Tally. You talk to the Council. We do not have much time."
pages.image: A girl with a silver hair streak leans over a table with a diagram, pointing at a line, while a tall boy in a navy jumpsuit and a small boy in a red hoodie look at her with serious, attentive expressions, a warm amber lamp glowing on the wall behind them.

pages.text:
"Who goes out there?" Voss asked. The question hung in the air, sharp and unyielding.

Lio answered before the silence could settle. "I do."

Voss shook his head, his ginger beard twitching with the motion. "No. It is not your call, and it is not mine. It is a decision that must be made based on experience, not on impulse." He trailed off, looking at Lio and then at Kess. "It needs to be made based on who is most likely to survive."

"I am the most experienced," Lio said, his voice tight and controlled. "I have done three EVAs. I know the suit, the tether, the checklist. I know the void."

"You are seventeen," Voss said. "I am forty-eight. I have done thirty EVAs. I know the void. I know what it feels like to be out there, alone, with the airlock door between you and death."

"Death is not the issue," Lio said, leaning forward. "The issue is time. I am faster. I am lighter. I can move in the suit without exhausting myself. You are heavy, Voss. Your suit will be a burden. You will be slower. And we do not have time for slowness."

Voss stared at him, the grease-stained grey coverall bunching at his shoulders. "You think I am too old?"

"I think you are too cautious," Lio said. "And caution is a luxury we cannot afford."

Kess put her hand flat on the table. "Stop." The word was quiet, but it landed with the finality of a heavy press locking into place. "You are both wrong. Lio, you are not going because you are fast. You are going because you are the only one who can. Voss, you are not staying because you are old. You are staying because you are the only one who can hold the line inside."

Voss frowned, his bushy beard darkening. "Hold the line?"

"The plan does not work if you are out there," Kess continued, her voice steady. "The plan works if you are in the pump house, watching the pressure, watching the temperature, watching the numbers. That is your job. That is your strength."

Voss looked at her, and a look of weary respect settled over his face, replacing the earlier suspicion. "The last time I sent someone out there," he said, his voice low and rough, "he made a mistake. A small one. A fraction of a second too late. He lost his left hand."

The room went silent, the hum of the workshop pumps seeming to grow louder in the stillness. Pim looked down at his hands, his mismatched socks shifting on the floor. Lio looked at Voss, and for the first time, his confidence wavered, the certainty in his eyes flickering like a grow-light under a power fluctuation.

"He survived," Voss added, after a pause. "But he never worked again."
pages.image: A bearded engineer and a tall boy in a navy jumpsuit face each other across a table, their expressions tense, while a girl with a silver hair streak places her hand on the table to stop the argument, a small boy in a red hoodie looking down at his hands.

pages.text:
Voss remained silent for a long moment, his gaze fixed on the napkin spread across the workbench, where their hastily sketched plans in grease and marker formed a small, chaotic world of lines and circles. He picked up his tea, took a slow sip, and set the cup down with a deliberate click against the wood.

"Lio will train for the EVA," he said, his voice low and steady. "Under my supervision. Every day, for two weeks. We will run the checklist, we will run the tether drills, we will run the emergency protocols until they are as natural to you as breathing. I will not let you go out there until I know, with absolute certainty, that your hands are steady and your mind is clear."

Lio nodded, his jaw tight, the muscles in his neck visible beneath his skin.

"Kess will run the heat calculations and mission control," Voss continued, turning his attention to her. "You will be in the pump house, watching the numbers. If the pressure drops, you call it. If the temperature rises, you call it. You are the eyes of the ship. You will not look away."

Kess felt a surge of something that was not quite confidence, but was close to it; it was the feeling of being trusted, of being part of a mechanism that required her precision. "I will not look away," she said, and meant it with every part of her.

"Pim will be the official biscuit officer," Voss said, without a trace of humor.

Pim blinked, his yellow hair-ties swaying. "Biscuit officer?"

"Yes. You will ensure that the team is fed. You will bring us soup, you will bring us water, you will bring us morale. It is a critical role. If we are hungry, our hands shake, and if our hands shake, we make mistakes. And we cannot afford mistakes."

Pim looked at his hands, then at Voss, his mismatched socks shifting slightly on the floor as he processed the gravity of the appointment. He stood up, straightened his red hoodie, and placed his hand over his heart with a seriousness that belied his age. "I accept the title of Biscuit Officer," he said solemnly. "I will not fail you."

Voss nodded, a faint, grudging respect in his eyes. "Good. We have a plan. We have a deadline. And we have a very large number of things that could go wrong. So let us go fix them, one by one, before they have the chance to break."
